utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, 6th of May, 2009. Good afternoon to Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Pusic. Good afternoon to you, General Praljak, and good afternoon to the Defence counsel, Mr. Scott, Mr. Stringer, and all their associates and the people assisting us. I'll first give the floor to the Registrar. He has an IC number for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 2D has submitted its response to the Prosecution's objections to their request for admission of exhibits tendered through Witness Dragan Juric. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1008. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Before we continue with the examination-in-chief, the Trial Chamber, through me, has three things to say. The first thing: The Trial Chamber invites General Praljak's Defence, through his counsel, Mr. Kovacic, to download, before the hearing, all the documents that he plans to put with their questions. All the documents have to be in the e-court system so that the Registrar can call them up. Of course, we settled the issue by using the ELMO, but in principle, it is better to send the document to the e-court system before the hearing begins. So make sure it is done. Secondly, with regard to time, in order to avoid any possible misinterpretation as to the way time is recorded, when a Judge puts a question on a given topic, obviously enough, the time is not going to be taken out of the accused's time. However, the accused has to give a concise and brief answer to the Judge's question. Last time, by way of an example, Judge Prandler asked a question on Croatia and Hungary, and Mr. Praljak answered close to half an hour. That's far too much. If the Trial Chamber is of the view that the answers are too long, we might take the time out of the overall time allotted to Mr. Praljak. So please, Mr. Praljak, do make an effort. Do try to answer briefly when the Judges put questions to you. Now, if, following a question that was ill put by the lawyer, or if it's a leading question, or if Mr. Praljak sort of answers all over the place, the time taken to settle the objection, because Mr. Stringer is bound to get on his feet and put an objection, that time is going to be taken out of the accused's time. It's not going to be taken out of the time given to Judges, especially if a Judge does intervene in order to correct the problem and invites the accused to answer, but then it is taken out of the time given to the accused. Thirdly, towards the end of yesterday's hearing we had an exchange of arguments on the fact that the Judges noted that General Praljak often sort of spilled over or went beyond the scope and went into general topics. There was a suggestion made by Mr. Karnavas. He invited Mr. Praljak and his lawyer to focus on the facts and possibly to go into general issues on a case-by-case basis. The Trial Chamber renews its invitation to Mr. Praljak. He is to answer questions especially based on facts, because facts are the primary concern of Judges. We expect Mr. Praljak, and it is in his own interest, to give us precise information on facts that he was given to know, that he knows, and that he's likely to give us information about, so that the truth can be established. Any speech that will go really all over the place will have to be focused again. Let me give you an example. If we are to deal with control of soldiers, we expect Mr. Praljak to tell us what is his first-hand knowledge and experience on the issue. We know that he went to the front-line, he told us so, and he can say, This is the specific problem I was faced with when I was on the front-line. There's no point in telling us about Hagel, Kierkegaard or Engels in order to speak about that topic. Do stick to the facts, because that's what we are interested in, because when we draft the judgement, we have to say whether the military commander did communicate to us specific facts. Any psychological or political reference in this instant case will have very little, if any, probative value. Therefore, the Trial Chamber once again invites the accused, as was pointed out yesterday by Judge Trechsel, to focus to the facts. There may have appeared some kind of divergence of views among the Judges, but that is not so. We all, each and every one of us, want General Praljak to focus on the facts. If at any time or at a given time he may say, Yes, in terms of command, I had to deal with drunkards for this or that reason, that he can say, but he's not supposed to start a theory on alcoholism. That is of absolute no interest whatsoever. So this is just by way of reminder so that the hearing can unfold as best as possible, to avoid incessant objections, for Mr. Praljak to be able to develop his line of defence in a serene and calm way, without being interrupted; so everyone can take notes and listen to him; so that his lawyer can ask questions of him in a clear fashion; so that the answers be brief and clear. All this first proves to be established. This is what I wanted to say, and I do hope that everybody understood me, everybody has funded the issue, and I hope, Mr. Praljak, that you will make an effort, keeping in mind primarily the following guide-lines: I have to focus on facts. I have to provide clear and brief answers. This is not a university campus. We cannot go on forever on each and every topic in the world. This is a criminal court, and it is a very specific case. We, as Judges, we have to make findings. That's the reason why you have to answer the questions that are put to you, without going astray into fields that may be of interest, but are very remote from the facts of the case. So I hope everybody got my message. Mr. Kovacic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to all. We understand your instructions, and we will do our best to comply with it, although to a large extent we have now completed our introduction in which we tried to indicate the general backdrop against which certain events unfolded. Just in order to inform the Chamber, the question was raised yesterday about what documents Mr. Praljak was referring to when he talked about the calculation regarding the shells that fell on East Mostar and the calculation based on SpaBat reports, and then also the artillery/ammunition expenditure by the JNA, or according to standards defined by the JNA. The numbers are IC00559. That's the first document, where Praljak quite simply calculated or added up all of the shells -- the amounts of shells recorded by SpaBat in their ECM reports in the second half of 1993. The other one is 3D01727, are the ammunition expenditures according to JNA standards, general standards used by armies, providing a general idea of what an artillery unit would normally use up in situations such as these. These are the document references, so you can have a look now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back a little or, rather, complete our discussion on a topic that arises from your CV. I would like to ask the Registrar to hand to us the folder entitled "CV" or biography, personal information.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that reaches us, I would like to thank the Judges, and I would like to explain that it was by no means my intention to cast my bales of wisdom around this courtroom. Everything I was trying to say and all the information that I was trying to get in had one motive at the root. I mean, a mental desire was to show what happened to us and what happened to others and to try to show the correlation between these events, why we did what we did, why we couldn't have done any better or why we couldn't have done any worse. I will try to abide by your instructions, but please do by all means understand that my intention was only this: To try to view a complex situation, such as a war, from the greatest possible number of different perspectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, several questions to go through. I think the fastest way to do this would be for you to go to the CV folder, biography folder, documents and all of your appointments and dismissals in 1993 in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Before that, I would just like to ask you a preliminary question. What was your status in 1992 in Bosnia and Herzegovina? As you have pointed out before, you spent some time there and then spent some time elsewhere. You would come and go throughout that time. What was your official capacity in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in 1992, it was on the 10th of April, 1992, that I was appointed commander of a front that we referred to as South-Western Herzegovina. I remained in that position, I believe, for a month and a half, after which a replacement arrived and I went back to Croatia to work as assistant minister for IPD.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you now please go to this folder that I handed to you. The first document that I'm about to show to you is P02604. This is an exhibit already. It has been tendered and admitted. Could you please just say, in a couple of words, what this document really is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an application in which I request the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia to enable me to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina, to fight there, as the aggressor by this time was very powerful already. I also asked for my dismissal from the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when exactly did you file this application?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please move on to the next document, 3D00278, another exhibit, but just in order to put everyone in the picture.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of July, 1993, our application was granted. A decision was made by the Personnel Administration section of the Defence Ministry of the Republic of Croatia, dismissing me or discharging me from myself duties with the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next document is P03683, and this should be seen jointly with 3D00279. Let's try to look at these two at the same time. The documents are identical, but I think I can allow myself to say, and this is not giving evidence, the first P document, as everyone has learned so far, is from packet communication, and the next one is the original signed by the person who produced the document. Can you please explain what that document means?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 24th of July, 1993, the supreme commander of the HVO, Mate Boban appointed me commander of the Main Staff of the HVO. In this document, Major General Milivoj Petkovic informs the units of the HVO of the HZ-HB that my appointment to the post of commander of the Main Staff of the HVO was made and that I was hereby appointed to that position by Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right, thank you. Next document, just to put this on the record clearly. As of that date when this information was forwarded, you were, de jure, commander of the Main Staff of the HVO of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next document up is P06235. Can you please look at that document. The 20th of September, 1993, what did you do then, or, rather, what did you request in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I submitted an application to the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of the Croatian Republic of the HB, Mate Boban. I forwarded the same document to the defence minister as well, although I don't really think he was the defence minister at the time, but the charge d'affaires of the Defence office. These errors, however, are something I tended to take in my stride. It wasn't written up with absolute accuracy. That was the nature of the times. We just didn't mind some of these small slip-ups and errors. I stated that a condition of discopathy was something that affected my health, my poor health at the time, and I requested to be dismissed as the Commander-in-Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO by the 15th -- by the 5th of November, 1993. I also said that by that date, I will have handed over all my duties to the deputy commander of the GS HVO, General Milivoj Petkovic, or another officer appointed to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think a question arises naturally here. General, before the Chamber poses the question, I think I might as well do that myself right away. From the end of July, throughout August, September and October, as we now see, you were a commander. You told us about your experience throughout that time about the war and all of that, yet here you state a medical condition as a reason for you leaving. What was your mental and physical condition after those three months of fierce fighting and war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to define my condition with any amount of precision. One couldn't really say that my poor health was the only reason for my decision to leave. I was quite tired. It had been a very demanding period. We hardly got any sleep at all, and the war raged on incessantly. The HVO at the time was an army facing a lot of problems. There was an offensive that had been launched by the BH Army across a very large area. There was the problem of getting supplies into Central Bosnia, into Vitez and Kiseljak. Another problem was getting the supplies through to Zepce. Most of the problems were supply problems. The greatest problem we faced was the attrition felt by the soldiers. There were too few soldiers in our ranks. The front-line was very broad, and there was overstretch as well. Mobilisation, itself, was a disaster, the simple reason being it wasn't possible to have a normal mobilisation implemented. Summons were issued, but if someone failed to respond, there was nothing we could do to force them to take up their posts. Anyone was free to do as they pleased, in one word. Anything that we might term state authority or civilian authority, or all of those bodies, were helpless and they could do nothing about that. No steps to take. The HVO, or what remained of it, the people still fighting were, to all practical intents, volunteers. Efforts were made by Bruno Stojic and by me, but they hardly yielded any substantial results. That was the one thing. The other thing was something that bothered me in a particular way. In a way, the influence of the municipalities and the municipal leaderships on the army had grown in the meantime. It was difficult and sometimes even impossible to get an order implemented. People were trying all sorts of tricks. Some of the municipalities not directly affected by the offensive coming from Uskoplje and so on and so forth were simply too glad not to provide soldiers for the front-line, and they didn't make enough of a general effort required to not lose the war, to not be defeated. The main duty of an operative commander in an army is not to lose a war, as simple as that, to not be defeated by whoever attacks you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please move on to the next document, 3D00280 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just go on with the question you've actually asked, Mr. Kovacic. It was to the health problems. You have said that you had cardiac arrhythmia and discopathy. Did you make that up or was there any evidence? Did you have medical records to support that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My condition goes back to before the war. I suffered from serious discopathy-related problems. There were times when I would spend 30 days entirely unable to move, just lying on the floor. The condition of my spine is still very poor, but I try to keep going. Even in the middle of war, I was sometimes strapped by poor mobility, unable to walk or move about, and I received all sorts of treatments by various people, who administered shots to improve my condition and so on and so forth. As far as my heart is concerned, physiologically speaking, my heart is all right, but there were problems there simply because of the enormous strain that I was under. But as this discopathy condition developed, the problem became quite serious. I was still up to the effort and the strain, and I would like to explain this later on, but there was now some sort of a lull and the Muslim offensive had lost momentum by this time. It hadn't quite been crushed yet, but had lost momentum. I believed that a replacement was a good idea at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document I called was 3D00280.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify what this document is about? It is a result of what, exactly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the result of a request that I made. The date we see is the 8th of November, 1993. Mate Boban, the Commander-in-Chief, relieves me of my duty. All the information is there. He hereby appoints Colonel Ante Roso as my replacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If we look at item 1, at paragraph 1 of this document, it seems to suggest that Boban relieved you of your duties pursuant to your own request, which is obviously the request we looked at several minutes ago about your illness, but he said as of the 29th of October, 1993, whereas the document itself bears the date of the 8th of November. Does that not mean, in practical terms, that the earliest you learned about this document was the 8th of November?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that is not correct. It reads pursuant to a personal request, the filing number dated the 29th of October. That was the date I filed my request, and then on the 8th of November my request was granted. There is no misunderstanding here at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. The 29th of October is the date of the document that you previously submitted. Okay, thank you very much. Paragraph 2, Boban hereby appoints a new commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a somewhat delicate question to ask you, but I have to do my job; and I can't ignore certain things. As you know, the Judges have been involved in this case file for years now. As a result, we are aware of several documents. We can see these documents that establish, in a clear fashion, that on the 29th of October, you asked to be relieved of your duty for health reasons. All the following documents are going to make your request more specific, going through the administrative channels, because you're going to be relieved of your post following your request. That's one way of reading these documents. But as a judge, I have to verify certain things. You know, as well as I do, that the attack on the village of Stupni Do occurred on the 23rd of October. That is six days before you requested to be relieved of your duty. Here in this courtroom we heard the US ambassador, remember him, and he said clearly - I'm quoting from memory - that they'd asked Tudjman to relieve the people who were responsible of their duties. There are two possibilities. I remind you that you are under oath and you said that you would tell the whole truth. Therefore, whatever you say may commit you. So two types of situations may occur. The first one is that you really were ill and indeed, as you said, you had to relinquish your position because it was very hard, you have to be on deck 24 hours a day, and as was said in this document, you felt you were not up to the task. That's one first way of looking at the reason why you left your position, but there may be another one, and I have to look into it with you. That second possibility is that as soon as the international community was informed of what happened in Stupni Do, you know there's feedback going through various channels, and we know that Mr. Tudjman was informed, also because he had secret services working for that very purpose, and he was perfectly in the know of everything that happened. Therefore, you were given to understand then that you had to go, and in order to avoid problems, the classic solution is to say that one is ill and one has to leave. So, Mr. Praljak, you are under oath today. What was the real situation on the 29th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, whatever I say under oath, so help me God, I really am saying the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Nobody, neither President Franjo Tudjman, nor Mate Boban, asked me to leave for any reason at all. It is true that the reasons, as stated, that is, discopathy and arrhythmia, are not the relevant reasons why I asked to be dismissed. About Stupni Do, this could hardly be the reason. I have nothing to do with Stupni Do. All the activities, until the last day or the eve before my departure, I signed an acceleration of my insistence that this be solved. General Petkovic was exhausted, and he wanted a few days of leave to go home, and I granted him that leave. The exact dates will be stated afterwards. And I signed that document on the day when I was dismissed. I believe it was the 8th of November, 1993. The true reason for my departure was that I did not approve the quantity or the huge effort -- or the efforts made to avoid losing the war. This refers primarily to the late Mate Boban and his organisational leadership of what was called the HZ-HB. I don't want to say that I did not approve of the policy that was -- of the time, because I was a soldier and he signed all relevant international agreements and so forth, but a great portion of the population did not take part in the war or didn't take part in a sufficient -- to a sufficient extent. It seemed like my boys and I were fighting for I don't know who. And there was this meeting in Split where I made a demand for Mate Boban to leave his function, because for one thing he was in Grude rather than in Mostar, the offices were in a poor state, and it all looked as if we were in a back woods. I criticised his organisational efforts, and among other things I demanded commissioners to be appointed for individual municipalities. There was a type of democracy that resulted in total chaos. For my whole life, or at least as long as I can think back, I was all in favour of democracy, but when you have meetings in municipalities, discussing pointless topics and drafting senseless letters, without making a real effort, and I can state from my personal experience that the limited attack was focused and that the will behind it was to reach the Adriatic coast, and these boys, and we're talking about the second year of warfare, were completely exhausted, and behind the front-line there was easy living going on. And you will be able to see, in the documents we're about to show, there were two meetings immediately before my departure, meetings of the army commanders, and these contained the demands that were made from the civilian authorities for us to avoid losing the war. Just let me finish, Your Honours. Jadranko Prlic opposed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Praljak. Let me stop you there, because you will have the opportunity to come back on this, but you fully answered my question. You told us that independently of your health, you also had a disagreement with Mr. Mate Boban. This is on the record. And you also told us, under oath, that your departure had absolutely nothing to do with what happened at Stupni Do, which was the purpose of my question. Now, as to the details and, you say, the two meetings in Split and so on, I'm sure we'll revisit the matter. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you should just finish your sentence, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to say something I consider quite significant. After the war, Ambassador Galbraith held a political speech, I believe it was in Slavonski Brod, as if he was in a banana republic. He was trying to show off his wit, trying to teach everybody --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we clarify whose clock this testimony is on, whether it's the Trial Chamber's or whether it's the accused's time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was my question. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time of the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote that this was not a decent thing to do, that we were a sovereign country, and that ambassadors even of our great and powerful countries cannot hold political speeches in public places and on squares. And Galbraith said, Why is this man, who brought down the Old Bridge, taking the floor and speaking? And -- but I was eventually the one to apply for being dismissed, and this has nothing to do with Stupni Do. I also wrote a letter to UNPROFOR. This has already been shown, but it will be additionally clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General Praljak, the next document is 3D00948. This is a hand-over document between you and General Roso. It is dated November the 9th. Tell me clearly how this hand-over took place. Was it on the 9th of November, how long it took, where it took place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This hand-over took place on November the 9th at 7.35 or 7.40 a.m. at Grude. There's my signature. Nothing to add there. And on the previous day, on the 8th of November, in the afternoon, around Livno I met General Roso, and I described the situation at the front-line to him and everything I considered important for that commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What did you do after signing this document on the 9th of November in the morning hours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sat in my car and drove home to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this document on the handing over of duties at 7.45, November 9, you told us earlier that the day before on November 8, you talked with General Roso about ongoing matters. As far as you remember, are you sure that you told him everything? Do you remember that you told him everything, that you drew him the full picture of what was happening, giving him details as to the positions of the HVO on the field, as to the problems occurring at the time, as to the operations that had to be conducted, maybe as to the sanctions that were to be taken? So when you handed over the duties, did you do it according to the state of the art?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all the data, all facts, I precisely gave to General Roso, and that wasn't difficult to do because he had been a member of the HVO before. He was a commander of Livno. He was also in Mostar after my departure, when it was liberated. So he was a man who knew the situation relatively well. He wasn't far from the events. And in the headquarters, in a room of the deputy chief of staff, General Matic, who was a retired general of the JNA, in his office he got an exhaustive account of mobilisation issues and what I knew about Stupni Do, so he was acquainted with everything that I considered important at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, let us just help the others to avoid asking unnecessary questions. When you're saying that General Roso had been in Mostar earlier, and you mentioned after your departure, which time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the transcript, this document, 3D00948, which we have just looked at, is identical to 3D06556, which is already an exhibit. General, the last document in this small set is 4D00834. I believe we've seen it before. So it's 4D00834. I'm being warned the one that I mentioned before, 3D00948, is identical to P06556. That is the correction that I wanted to make, this latter document being an exhibit already. Let us return to 4D00834. According to our registers, this is the last document that you signed in your capacity of -- sorry. Yes, in fact, it's correct. My copy is poor. Please say if it is or it isn't.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that was drafted for General Milivoj Petkovic for the simple reason I can explain. When I was appointed the chief of the General Staff of the HVO, I had been down there a little earlier in June and early July, until November the 10th. I was a Boksevica, but we'll come to that, in 1993, and I knew the military situation thoroughly. It is important to explain that, speaking about the situation. There was always the tendency to put things into order formally, so -- and there is written evidence of that, et cetera. The military situation on the ground was very bad for us. I organised a general staff which probably wasn't in existence anywhere else. That was a special problem to General Matic, who was used to things as they were done in the JNA. There was the chief of the General Staff, the deputy, then there was also the commander of the General Staff and his deputy, and all that because you may want to think that the commander of an army sits in an office, that he gets information, issues orders, and these orders are obeyed, but that wasn't really how it was. And if things aren't like that in reality, then you cannot pretend that things are what they are not. At that moment, the commanders, myself, Petkovic, and the others, had to go to the field, leave their offices, and forget about usual procedures and impressions of the army as something that functions perfectly. I understood, which will be corroborated by witnesses, that our main problem would be the attack by the BiH Army from the direction of Uskoplje and Rama, which would have meant a complete defeat of the HVO, so I went there. The area of Mostar and the south should have become the responsibility of the Chief of General Staff. What was his name again? Tole. And General Petkovic was to concentrate on avoiding the fall of Kiseljak, Vares and Central Bosnia. I even appointed him as the negotiator because there were many people from the international community and UNPROFOR and monitors and journalists. Everybody wanted to talk to you and have meetings. So it wasn't simply possible in wartime conditions, especially given the situation as it was at the time. After returning from Kiseljak, General Petkovic was really exhausted, and he applied for five or six days of leave. I didn't give him as much, I gave him less, but he was in a way much better acquainted with the situation, and I signed this command. I believe it was the last command I signed -- the last order I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that you left for Zagreb on the 9th of November. My question to you, General, is whether later, during the war, you ever returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In January 1994, but without being appointed, I came of my own accord. I went to Uskoplje because the situation hadn't improved -- didn't improve after my departure. On the contrary, I believe that it even aggravated. The Army of BiH again were growing stronger than the HVO around Uskoplje. I think that I can say with justification that I was a good commander and that the soldiers appreciated me and were fond of me – because I spent most of my time with them, and they asked me to come and help them; and I came in January 1994. I reported to General Roso and the commander of the zone of operation who at the time was General Vrbanac, and I stayed there and fought, and I think the results were good. This lasted for three or three and a half weeks. And when our success became obvious, in the tactical sense, Alija Izetbegovic suggested a truce again. So whenever the ABiH was successful, its commander and Alija Izetbegovic would break the cease-fire that was in place, but whenever we had a tactical advantage, such as in Uskoplje, they propose a cease-fire, which I accepted, and we also respected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A very tiny question, Mr. Praljak. When you went back in November, how were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wore military clothes; no insignia, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No insignia of your grade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this is the first time I hear about this. So you told us that you came back to Uskoplje in January 1994, and now you're telling us that you fought for three weeks, but I had -- I thought I understood that on November 9, when you went back to Zagreb, you were reintegrated into the Croatian military structure because as you told us earlier, you said you were to be working on the archives. I'm sure you'll tell us later on, what you did during that period of time, but then for three weeks you suddenly leave your official job in Croatia. Did you get a leave of absence or were you -- was it a desertion or were you on vacation? How did it happen that you suddenly managed to leave your job and go for another country for three weeks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's exactly what I tried to speak about in the introduction. If you separate things like this, one country, another country, et cetera, I tried to explain that there was -- in Croatia, there was one theatre of war, but I was also a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I did not desert, and I didn't take leave either, but according to the basic principle in force in the Croatian Army, namely, that if a volunteer wants to go to fight to Bosnia-Herzegovina, he will be enabled to do so, for the simple reason that such was the general attitude, so there was no coercion, there was no order to do so, but whoever wanted to go to fight, to Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croats or Muslims, were enabled to do so and their place -- their position was waiting for them upon their return. So this was in force for everybody else, including myself. And after returning to Zagreb, I was asked to set up the archives of the Croatian Army, because the document that there was was in -- completely disorderly. I told them that I know nothing about archiving, but what I can do is make an effort to gather -- collect as much material as possible, so I can be in charge of collecting documents and then I will find people who know what to do then. So we first made a manual on archiving, and then we got facilities in a barracks in Zagreb that was suitable for archiving. Then we had to collect three-dimensional objects, as well as films, tapes, et cetera. But when I again learned that the situation was relatively critical and that a breakthrough was imminent, I went there of my own free will. If the Croatian state had wanted to sanction me, it could have done so, but there was no will to do so. Anyway, nobody could have stopped me from going there, because I considered Bosnia-Herzegovina my home, as well as Croatia, and you cannot divide this war into one -- one war into two separate wars. This mechanical separation that you are applying, as a Westerner, Your Honour, resulted in the attitude, Okay, let's pacify the situation in Croatia, and then we can turn to Bosnia-Herzegovina. But this war wasn't waged by countries; it was waged by the JNA and the Serbian political thought, directed against anybody who was not Serb, be they Muslims, Croats, or Slovenians at the beginning of the war. This war didn't have a character as the thing you think it has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, I cut you short. You say it was of your own free will. Fine. But you can imagine that for a Westerner, and this gives rise to many questions, well, you told us, you know, that for Westerners, it's very hard to understand a number of things. It's true that it's very hard to understand all this, but I'm sure that we'll be enlightened in due time. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just one thing on the transcript. We've gone rather far, but I can locate it relatively easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, when you were answering the question about the document, the last one that you signed, 4D00834, which is on page 19, lines 7 to 8, you spoke about Boksevica. The transcript reads that you had been there, I mean Boksevica, before in June, July, up until November.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Until approximately the 12th of July only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear, then.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a brief addition. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, this goes against my time. General de Gaulle didn't stick to the decisions of the French government either when he decided who to fight and where. He led his troops. When he was ordered not to enter Paris, he was ordered by Eisenhower, he sent Leclaire and the 3rd Army to enter Paris because it was his town and his country, and he didn't heed orders not to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after this departure to BiH in January 1994, you never returned to that country until up to the Dayton Accord?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's wrong. I returned when we were liberating Bihac. General Blaskic was the chief of General Staff then. I was asked to do so. The boys asked me to come and be with him while he was doing it, and that's what I did, and I lingered for about two weeks. The liberation of Kupres was done together with the ABiH, which came from the north. That is after the Washington Agreement. And we started liberating the Livno field, the right side of it, and then I returned to Zagreb again, to my work. And just to finish, I took part in the Storm operation in the area from Hrvatska Kostajnica to Dvor Na Uni without any high position as a simple soldier again, a private; and I entered Dvor Na Uni with the first tank, and I put the Croatian flag on the bridge which is on the border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was present when Serbian tanks were crushing carts, et cetera, driving over them, leaving Knin; and then I stayed for a while to see to it that the transportation infrastructure be repaired. I took care of the remaining Serbs, put them up, protected them, supplied them with food. I was with my own lads because I had previously fought by their side for 6 months in Sunja, I knew all those soldiers and they had confidence in me, although I had no commanding position. And that was the end of my wartime engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to make the time-frame clear --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with Bihac. I was talking about Hrvatska Kostajnica and Dvor Na Uni.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Earlier, when you were talking about Kupres --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was talking about the liberation of Kupres and the right side of the Livno field, Livanjsko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's the action which you ran together with General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I know now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that's between your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another odd thing. You spoke about what you did as part of the Storm operation. That's a new thing for me as well. But to avoid any mistake, the Storm operation was carried out by the Republic of Croatia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Operation Storm was carried out by the Republic of Croatia, but it was extended also to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On the 9th of November, you returned to Zagreb. I guess you had a rank then. What was your rank in the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I finished the war as a colonel general, but when I returned to BH, I did not have that rank yet. I was major general then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was very specific. On the 9th or 10th of November, 1993, what was your rank, your precise rank in the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were major general. And now you told us that this part of Operation Storm, you were on the first tank, you put up the flag, and you said, I was a simple soldier. Well, that's where I fail to understand anything at all. How can a general be a simple soldier, standing on a tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply, Your Honour, you wanted facts from me all the time, and now I'm giving you facts. You now adjust your theory to the facts. The theory of the army that I understand you want is not a good theory. The fact is, and we're talking now about 1995, the Operation Storm is beginning, I am still a Croatian soldier, but I have no position, no particular duty in that operation. The reason is, among other things, that the harangue that I was the one who had destroyed the Old Bridge gained humongous dimensions, and even President Franjo Tudjman believed it, so I addressed a letter to him where I said that I may appear before this Court, or perhaps not, that I would end up on trial; but in any case I had participated in that war for a long time by then, and when the operation started I joined in. I didn't care whether I was there as a general or not. I did not care for the way things were done in the French Army, or the Foreign Legion, or any other army. I went to the place I had been before, near Sunja, to Hrvatska Kostajnica, and of course the boys, the troops that I had been with earlier for six months, were happy to see me, and of course they would obey me. Even commanding officers would obey me. I knew that they would accept my advice. I was not exactly on a tank, to be precise. I was walking along a tank. We wanted to avoid the column of Serbs fleeing to Bosnia and Herzegovina. We did not want to cut through the column. We watched their own tanks rolling over the bridge and rolling over the civilians, without any care for their lives. And when I entered Dvor Na Uni River, I asked for a flag and I hoisted it there on the bridge. I was very happy, very satisfied, very proud; and then I stayed on for another two days because, of course, after the excitement of a successfully finished operation, there is a lot of organisational, infrastructural work to be done, dead bodies to be removed, roads to be repaired; and there is a feeling of general relief, but I never relaxed. I just took up a new kind of work. I issued instructions that were obeyed, although they were not formal instructions or orders as they are normally given in the army and as you understand the army to function. But I said to the men around me: “Let's protect them, get food, let's organise accommodation for these Serbs, let's clear this road, et cetera.”

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. I think we can now move on to another subject, the subject that you had spoken about very briefly in your introductory statement. [In English] I would ask the usher to come here to take the binder. [Interpretation] I'd like to move to the subject of the developments -- political developments in Croatia in 1989 and 1990, the establishment of political parties, and your engagement therein, if any. It's the binder at the very bottom. You're not going to go through documents, General. First of all, I'd like you to tell the Trial Chamber whether you got involved into this political turmoil in those times of change.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me speak, will you? I belonged to that category of citizens of the Republic of Croatia who wanted, desired, and thought that Yugoslavia, as we knew it, would break up and that Croatia would become an independent democratic country that would join the group of Western democracies. We believed in Western democracies. We believed that democracy is a name we could and were able to accomplish and that we were ready for. I was ready for it, and I was quite prepared, without any pathos, to sacrifice my own life for it. I said to the Judge before I can bring -- and I wanted the Judges to understand that whatever I said about Oluja and the Operation Storm, and Boksevica and anything, all that I can corroborate by witness testimony, and I have witnesses to bring. For each of my statements, upon the request by the Court, I can produce concrete evidence. And before the war, I told everyone who was willing to listen, at great length and very insistently, that there would be a war. I went so far as to calculate the number of victims that the Croatian side would have to suffer, and I said that Croatia would lose at least 50.000 people, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, your counsel put a question to you. It was a very interesting question for us Judges. Your counsel would like you to describe the political situation in Croatia in 1989 and 1990 for our information. As you know, in the indictment there is a JCE, alleged JCE, including Croatian political leaders, so it would be very interesting to have -- to know exactly what the political situation was like in Croatia, where Tudjman came from; what was his political orientation; to know where you were also. And your counsel is putting this question to you, but now you're going astray. Could you please get back on track and answer the question put to you by your counsel because it is a very important question for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am listening to my counsel, but of course it did not begin really in 1988 or 1989. It started long before that and never ceased. There had always been people who ended up in prison in Croatia, beginning with 1918 [as interpreted], and it was not a small number. It was an ongoing process of mutiny. Franjo Tudjman appeared at that time on the Croatian stage. He had been in prison before. Marko Veselica, also a new figure, had been in prison for ten years. Seks had also been in jail. Vlado Veselica, who led the HSLS, had been in prison. Most of the people who appeared in the political arena at that time had served jail sentences of 10 or 15 years, and then their moment came. They realised that the possibility finally arose for them to realise their political dream. And the other thing is that after Tito's death, Yugoslavia started crumbling like a house of cards. There were huge problems in Kosovo that they stifled back in the 1980s, crushed the demonstrations in the mines. Then they changed the Constitution. It's impossible to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I recall that you have been warned you are here as a witness. Mr. Kovacic, your lawyer, asked you about the situation in 1988-1989 in Croatia. That is a time when you were there, so you can describe facts. Instead of doing this again, you've done something quite different, which we've told you several times that must not do. You posit, you give us a speech as if you were here as a historical expert, but you are not. You are here, as you know and as you have decided, as a witness. So I must insist on what the President already told you. You must not give us historical lectures about what happened in 1918, but you must say what, according to your personal experience, the political situation was in Croatia in 1988 and 1989.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, if you find someone who had been involved in politics in any era at any time -- but please let me speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Praljak, and you are not to argue. Every time a Judge tells you something, you argue, you talk back. This is -- in substance, it is a behaviour which could be regarded as contempt of Court, because it is a lack of respect. It is not for a witness to criticise the advice that Judges give them, particularly if the advice is a recall of the rules which every witness is obliged to follow. And as the Chamber has decided, it also applies to you. So, please, do not start arguing with me, this is not correct, but follow -- answer the question your own counsel has put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just offer one suggestion, because it seems to me that Mr. Kovacic is highly skilled and knows where he wants to take the general, and my guess is that he and the general have prepared, and they know where they want to get together. Rather than asking what's probably a pretty broad question to the general, What was the political situation during those two years, perhaps Mr. Kovacic could lead -- and I don't mean by leading questions, but by asking a series of questions that would elicit shorter answers. He could narrow what would be the answers that they're trying to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you've listened very keenly to what Mr. Stringer said, because he, too, tries to contribute to a useful examination of the witness, so he's asking you or inviting you to ask more specific questions, even to a certain extent leading questions, to make things easier. Of course, we'll be watchful, but you have some leeway, so that Mr. Praljak does remain on track. Of course, it could be interesting to know what happened in 1980, but as was said very well by Judge Trechsel, we are interested in 1988 and 1989 because this is going to foreshadow what is going to happen in 1991, so let's remain within that framework. You have ten minutes left before the break, Mr. Kovacic. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. Just one remark. On two occasions, the general said that this political process had been ongoing from 1980 onwards, and he named the persons who got involved in the political life in Croatia in 1989, and he named a number of people, said that those people had served time in jail, and then felt that now was the time of change, and those were two introductory sentences in response to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the right to ask you a question. Do you want the truth from me or do you want stereotyped truth? If you want stereotyped truth, then you don't need me. I participated in these events, and they have a complexity, a dimension that is impossible to reduce to simple formulas. That is simply not true. What you're asking from me is not the truth. The responses to your questions will not be the truth, because this did not start in 1988 or 1989, it started a long time before. Your Honour Judge Trechsel, it is not my intention to be contemptuous of the Court in any way. All I am trying to do is to avoid reducing a very, very complex situation to a model which would not reflect the truth. But finally, at the end of the day, there are thousands of books about that. If you don't need me, you can read the books. I'm just trying to paint the picture of the first appearance on the stage of persons who would later become leaders of parties. Don't treat me like this. I'm not an ameba here. I don't want to show any contempt of the Court, all I want is my evidence to be clear, exhaustive, and correct. When the whole of Yugoslavia is on fire, when everything is in turmoil, in a flux, I cannot produce the kind of answer you are trying to elicit from me. Let’s admit this book, this Djonlic, show him some things and end of story. I have prepared it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the Trial Chamber does not disagree with you on this issue, but we know that you're going to call an expert. This expert in history is going to testify, and I'm sure that he'll revisit these topics; all the more reason for you to really focus on the substance, you see. So really focus on what is essential, because we'll return to such topics. And Mr. -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1988, 1988, autumn of 1988. We meet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I cannot remain silent. I must protest. I think it is absolutely incorrect, the way you speak to me and try to give me lectures on what I have to do, and asking me questions. This is incorrect, and I must state it, and I have now stated it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, please answer. If you are of the view that you did not offend anybody, just say so. I have noticed that there may be some mistakes in translation that may lead to misunderstandings, so if you want to say that you did not mean to offend anybody, I think you said so, and say it again in order to avoid any misunderstanding. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. As I understood General Praljak, I don't believe he was trying to be offensive in any way, shape, or form, although something may have been lost in translation. As I understood it, he was quite respectful to Judge Trechsel, though Judge -- General Praljak wished to point out that, one, he was a participant during those events. He's not speaking as a historian, although we're talking about historical facts or historical issues which, of course, lead up to the events later on. And because he lived through that period, he's trying to put context as to what will ultimately follow. Having said that, I think Mr. Stringer is quite right, that perhaps if the questions are more narrowly fashioned, we can go step by step. Otherwise, it gives the impression that there is some sort of a historical dialogue going on, or monologue, and that seems to be the sense of confusion. And with that, perhaps we could take an early break and consequently perhaps readjust the questions for the best approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I was very clear. I said very clearly that it couldn't be furthest from my mind, and I don't know why it wasn't interpreted, to show any contempt or disrespect to the Court. It was simply impossible to understand me in that way. You must have misunderstood me, Judge Trechsel. I simply do not have it in me. On my part, there is no disrespect or contempt of the Court. I am simply on tenterhooks here. There is no historian who could know these things better than I, who lived them for 30 years. I am the expert in these matters. I lived -- I worked through that situation for 30 years, and no historian writing a tacit account of that would be able to show you all the finer points of what actually happened there. And from now on, if you want me, I will go giving you my account in bullet points. In 1988, the first gatherings, the first rallies started. Will you give me five more minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just react.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The question was you, Judge, mentioned earlier we would go on break, and now I'm confused. Should General Praljak continue or we go on break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think we're in a pre-break phrase of rounding up the issues that are pending. In my language, one calls this shooting down the cows that are flying in the air. Mr. Praljak, you have just evidenced the point that I was making. You have said, I am the best expert. I'm not disputing that, Mr. Praljak. Who am I to -- I'm not an expert in this, and I will accept that you may be an expert. But these criminal procedures, they are always a bit formal, maybe even formalistic, and the fact is that your role here is that of a witness and not that of an expert. The Rules of Procedure make a clear distinction between the two. The regulations are in different Rules, and it is our duty and our way to serve the fairness of the trial that we insist on these Rules being respected. I quite understand that this is unpleasant for you. You must feel like in a harness, but that's what all witnesses, unfortunately, must experience. And it may be a new experience for you, I can very much imagine. I can even sympathise with your feelings, absolutely. I might be torn apart similarly if I were in your place. But then perhaps you would be sitting here and recalling the Rules to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have seen, with these documents that are lying here below, the orders, what was done, et cetera. On these questions, I can answer "yes" or "no." If Mr. Kovacic goes on putting his questions, we'll go very quickly. That part is simple. You went there, you did this, you were ill. That's quite straightforward. But this attempt to make a summary finally makes me explode. How can I compress things any further? If you go on compressing, you are no longer in the area of truth. The compression is too high. There is no model to follow. That's what troubles me here. When we get to the documents, where it's easy, I was here, I did this, I made this order, that's straightforward and quite simple, but the situation in 1988 and 1999 -- sorry, 1989, that is very complex. But I'll try to make that shorter. Thank you very much. I will abide by your instructions as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a break now, but please think it over for a few seconds. Imagine that you are an American citizen and I ask you to tell me -- tell us what the situation was in 1988 and 1989 in the USA. Well, the witness would say, Well, there were two parties, the Republican Party and the Democrats. That's all. He's not going to speak about the war of secession, the Civil War, or the war against Mexico. That's all. We're going to break for 20 minutes. We shall then resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I believe that Mr. Khan had something to say for a few minutes on the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, firstly good afternoon. Many thanks for giving time. It's a very short matter indeed. We are intending today to file two motions for the admission of documentary evidence. There is a third matter, a motion for the admission of documentary evidence relating to cooperation and relation between the HVO and ABiH forces. It's only six pages in length, but we are seeking the admission of about 85 to 90 documents. It's in relation to that motion that I am seeking an extension of time to file by 10.00 tomorrow morning, at the latest. I have taken the liberty of discussing the matter with my learned friend Mr. Stringer, and there's graciously no objection by the Prosecution. Your Honours, I would ask for this extension. I can give further reasons should that be needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has consulted and is granting you leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Khan. Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, back to what I asked you before, 1988-1989 in Croatia, the setting up of political parties. Can you please tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, briefly. 1988, Yugoslavia, Milosevic in power. The SANU memorandum on the political desires has been tabled already. In a financial sense, there is the money being printed in Belgrade, leading to the breakdown of the entire financial system. Inflation is galloping, the economy is in tatters. Large-scale meetings of Serbs in Kosovo. The autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina is abolished, which is an attack on the Constitution of the socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. In Croatia, February 1989, a group of people meets, about 150 of them, in the Croatian Writers Association, with me in attendance. The Croatian Democratic Party is founded or being founded. It is not quite there yet, because there can be no multi-party system in Yugoslavia yet. The first party to be established in Croatia, within the framework of the League of Socialists, there is no law providing for a multi-party system. There is very broad-ranging organisation called the Socialist Alliance in Yugoslavia, and then within that alliance some legal loop-holes were identified through which the HSLS established its right to be a separate party within the alliance. The HSLS is led by Slavko Goldstein, a Croatian Jew, with members such as Budisa [phoen], one of the leaders of the student movement back in 1971, who served five years in prison; Vlado Gotovac, a writer, six years in prison. The HDZ is made up, for the most part: Tudjman, two or three years in prison; Mesic, a year or so in prison; Seks, prison; Milas, prison; Muhamed Zulic [phoen], a Muslim, he was in prison too, I believe; Perica, 14 years in prison. At the beginning, Marko Veselica, too, was a member of the HDZ, and he had spent 11 years in prison. The HHS, the Croatian Peasants Party, is led by Stipac, an elderly gentleman who served three terms in prison during the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. Next, he was imprisoned by Ante Pavelic's regime, and lastly he was in prison during Tito. Another man involved was Zvonimir Cicak, four years in prison. Croatia's League of Communists was led by Racan and the Croatian People's Party by Savka Dapcevic-Kucar, a former president of Croatian's Communists. Another person involved was Tripalo. They were replaced and thrown out in 1971 during the Croatian Spring. Another person involved is Srecko Bijelic, a Serb, and other people too, but those were the most important people there. When the HDZ was established, there was a schism caused by rivalry between Marko Veselica, who at the time had not left prison yet, but he was banned from public appearances and public speech. That was one of the provisions of the law that applied at the time. So there was Marko Veselica and his brother, Vlado Veselica, and they founded the Croatia Democratic Party. I, too, was a member of that party. Another high-ranking position in the party was held by Djordje Pribicevic, a Serb. I was the main secretary of the party. 1989 went by. As these parties were being established, there were lots of talks, meetings, field trips, just what pre-election campaigns normally looked like, except this was a different thing altogether. Needless to say, everything that went on at the time ran counter to the existing positive laws of Yugoslavia. In other words, under the laws that applied, had the state been a solid state and had Tito survived, we would all have ended up in prison, serving long-term sentences. Nevertheless, a breakup of that country was in progress and no one could summon up enough power to send these people to prison. Therefore, this would be the briefest possible summary of the situation as it prevailed back at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is something that we have here, and we'll be showing this DVD to the Chamber in a couple of minutes. I have something that the Judges might be interested in, although you have, to some extent, announced the topic. But please try to briefly tell the Chamber why you, Slobodan Praljak, decided to get involved in this political ferment and why did you join this party?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my own free will and personal desire. There's just something else I would like to add. At the time, party statutes were being drawn up, political declarations explaining what the ambitions were, what the objectives were. When the statutes were being drawn up and all the announcements, which amounted to an enormous amount of work, obviously, we were collecting material from other parties abroad -- from Germany, from Italy, because we are now untrained in a way, we are not experts, we are putting all this stuff together. We're studying it, translating it. We know what the general framework is supposed to be, but how do we write up the statute of a modern Democratic Party. So this was just in progress and we were adding things as we went along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, just to avoid any misunderstanding, as far as the essence of all these things that went on at the time is concerned, you talked about all these persons who were now involved, actively involved in politics, and you told us about their prison terms. What were their crimes? What did they end up in prison for? Were they robbers, thieves, or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Before answering this question, General Praljak, you did not answer the question put to you by your counsel, and it was a very important question. Actually, it's at the very heart of your own personality. The question was: Why did you join this party? You didn't give us the reasons. Did you join the party for this or that reason? That's what we want to know. Why did you join this party, this party and not another party, and to what end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honour, I wish to say this: There were only very small differences between the parties. I thought the question might be raised later on, so I have with me the statutes of those parties and their platforms. It was all along the same lines; democracy, freedom, freedom of press, freedom of speech, democratic electoral system, multi-party system, and then as part of that, what sort of economy, free market economy, free market investments. In one word, the political system adopted by France, by Switzerland, and all the other Western countries. We wanted to become a Western democracy. It was always about the West, and everybody kept harping on about the West ad nauseam. That was the basis, the legal system being introduced, freedom, democracy. All of the parties invariably talked about civic rights, about national rights, the highest possible standards based on a European model related to national minorities, ethnic minorities, and all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Your counsel should move on to another question, but if he is not doing that, I will, myself, put the question that I believe he should have put to you. Obviously, he doesn't have the question at hand, so I'll put it to you. You just told -- you just gave us your reasons; democracy, freedom, freedom of press, freedom of speech, electoral system, multi-party system, so forth and so on, a freedom market, investments and so on. Now, I'm going to put this question to you, and I believe that Mr. Kovacic should have put it to you. Maybe the Prosecutor will also put it to you, but I'm trying to save time. Did you join this party for the purpose of the Greater Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honours, at the time it wasn't about Greater Croatia. We weren't even discussing leaving Yugoslavia at the time. The reasoning at the time was still about Yugoslavia being restructured as a confederative community. It was about greater rights for Croatia as part of that confederacy. More money because too much money was being taken away. It was still about Yugoslavia surviving as a confederacy, with the introduction of a multi-party system, parliamentary system, with free market economy being introduced. The thought hadn't even occurred to anyone. No one thought to speak of anything beyond that at the time. That was where we stopped. None of us believed it would be that simply to leave Yugoslavia. All we were asking for was a restructuring effort. Greater Croatia, Your Honours, no one ever uttered a single word about anything like that. The thought never occurred to anyone at all. I assert that without a shadow of a doubt. No one ever, and one must bear in mind that I was among the 100 or 200 people at the time, in that country who were involved in everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps to avoid any further questions and to make matters perfectly clear to everyone, you were specifically involved and were formerly a secretary of the party that was called HDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the full name was Croatian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. And then what I asked you before. You've mentioned quite a number of persons who became political leaders or party leaders who had served prison terms. Why? What were their crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their crimes were verbal offences, for the most part, and as their indictments at the time read, attempts to undermine the constitutional order. I think Ms. Alaburic would be better placed than me to say what this was all about. Enemy propaganda, I think that was the charge often raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were convicted on one charge, six months; and then the next one on enemy propaganda three years; and then the next one attempts to undermine the constitutional order, six years.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very precisely defined system, and specific sentences were touched, and specific crimes. And Tudjman, ex-Communist; Mesic, ex-Communist; Seks, ex-Communist; Marko Veselica, ex-Communist; Vlado Veselica, ex-Communist; Goldstajn, Communist. Just a minute, please. Cicak, no; Racan, Communist; Tripalo, Communist; Savko Dadcevic, Communist; Srecko Bijelic, Communist; Djordje Pribicevic, Communist. So in a way, all of them -- most of them, because there were some who weren't, but most of them were ex-Communist renegades, apposites, people who had clashed with the system, or reformed Communists, which we used to call them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've sped up somewhat, probably in a desire to save time. I think the best thing to do now would be to play the DVD that is next up, which tells us about this effort to reform and restructure political parties, and then I think Mr. Praljak can shed some light on that additionally. The number for that video is 3D03140. [In English] Is there a technical problem, Mr. Registrar? If there is something which would take a couple of minutes, I can go with something else, and then we can come back.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. Just to note that I've called in the technician to come and look at it to find out what the problem is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask, Mr. Kovacic, you have prepared and distributed a file with transcripts and surrogate sheets for video material; would it be helpful for us to look at one of the elements in that file?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes and no. If I remember correctly, the video has subtitles, and you have the transcript in front of you, the Croatian. The English is not necessary. But this is a short video, a total of 16 seconds, the first portion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I perhaps meanwhile be allowed to say what this is about? On the one hand, tensions were mounting throughout Yugoslavia. On the other, Croatia's League of Communists gradually stopped refusing the thought of introducing the multi-party system to Croatia, particularly after the rift at the Congress. The League of Communists stood up to Milosevic, who wanted to gain power over all the Communists in Yugoslavia, and then the Slovenes walked out, as did the Croats. After that, the time was ripe in Croatia, so Croatia's League of Communists, through its own state organs, of which it was in full control, made the decision to go ahead with the multi-party system in Croatia. All of the parties were now there to merely put their signature under this fact, to corroborate this fact. I was appointed on behalf of all these parties to give a brief speech, which I did. I thanked everyone. I remember exactly what I said at the time, although I think the whole thing got erased somewhere or other. I said this, specifically: that I was happy that Croatia's League of Communists, after 30 something or 40 years, had ceased to be illegal and has now finally become a legal party in Croatia, because Croatia's League of Communists was for the first time registered as a political party. When they had been in power, there was absolutely no need for them to deal with the legal niceties of the situation. The other thing that I said was, Now comes a time when the rest of us no longer need to be anti-Communists, a time has come when we can simply be non-Communists. This is an essential difference, because on the one hand we had the one-party system, and I opposed that system. I was anti-system, in a sense, and now Croatia's League of Communists were one of the many options that the citizens had to choose from. I now became a non-Communist, no longer an anti-Communist. I now considered them to be legal, legitimate. I believed that a person had the right to choose to be a Communist, to have their own party, to choose their own platform, as any other party, they could rally the popular support behind them, go to elections, and then if they win it, fine, they may go on governing, but for a four-year term and not ad infinitum. And then after a four-year period, there would be another election. That is what I said a couple of sentences, that is how I addressed all those people. I do remember that with great clarity, because this was a momentous event in Croatia at the time. A small detail to illustrate something, Your Honours. The TV crew who was supposed to record this were late, and then I had to go back several times because the first time around they were late and then the next time around the camera had not warmed up enough for them to actually produce the footage. But up until that point, up until that time when this finally became legal, joining those parties was an offence, it was illegal, and people were fearing reprisals. When, in the evening news on TV that night, it was announced that these parties had now become legal, people started joining these parties on a massive scale, and the overall amount of political activity in Croatia intensified to a very large extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the technology is now ready for us to proceed with the video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the very act, the signing of the document, and this is me addressing the people there. There is no sound. The sound was erased. There, you could see the representatives of these parties. It was a brief clip. This is from "Vreme" [indiscernible], a Croatian TV show, showing bits of this documentary. I don't know why the sound is no longer there. It's one of the mistakes that Your Honour Judge Antonetti asked me about. Why -- and an assumption why that was not taken? Because the TV did not have the tape, so they erased the sound. Apart from that, Your Honours, as commander in Sunja - I had been commander for two months - my first salary was 80 German marks, the equivalent of 80 German marks, simply because there wasn't enough money to go around Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
